ideas: A 'poor' art against the art system and the consumer object, made with elementary materials such as earth, wood, rags, stones and water.
The artist as a free guerrilla who chooses where to fight and what to use.
Energy, process and the presence of the body, as in works by Kounellis, Merz, Anselmo and Pistoletto.
manifesto.system: No sequencer and no synthesiser presets: only four poor materials and the energy of your body. Every sound comes from simple physical models of a wire, a stone, a drop or a rubbed rag.

design.name: Bruno Munari
design.who: Bruno Munari, Italian artist, designer and educator
hallmarks: Playful experiments with very simple means: paper, holes, folds and light
Clear geometric shapes in primary colours, with lots of white
Design for children, games and learning by doing
works: Useless Machines (from the 1930s)
Illegible Books (from 1949)
Campari poster, Declinazione grafica del nome Campari (1964)

title: Databend
idea: Bend the raw data of your sample: shift its bytes, flip its bits, swap and repeat its blocks, and listen to the medium break open.
how: Press PLAY. Your sample is turned into raw data (bytes) and played back as a loop. Each operation edits that data directly, as if you had opened the file in a text editor: SHIFT (moves the byte alignment, so the samples are read wrongly), FLIP (inverts random bits), SWAP (exchanges two blocks), STUTTER (repeats a block), 8-BIT (reads it as cheap 8-bit audio) and ZERO (wipes a block). Each operation stacks on the last. The display shows the data as coloured pixels. Repeating the same operation over and over turns the glitch into a style, and the machine warns you. UNDO steps back and CLEAN restores the original.

manifesto.name: Glitch Studies Manifesto
manifesto.author: Rosa Menkman
manifesto.where: published in Amsterdam and Cologne in 2010; later expanded in her book The Glitch Moment(um) (2011)
ideas: The glitch is a break that reveals the medium itself: its materials, protocols and hidden assumptions.
Resist the myth of the perfect, noiseless channel and the idea that progress means ever more transparent technology.
Once a glitch is repeated and designed, it can harden into a style or commodity, and stop being a glitch.
manifesto.system: You don't process sound with effects. You break the data that carries it, and the warning when you repeat yourself is the manifesto's point that a glitch turned into a preset is no longer a glitch.

design.name: Wolfgang Weingart
design.who: Wolfgang Weingart, German typographer and teacher at the Basel School of Design
hallmarks: Swiss typography broken open: layered film, screens, stepped and spaced type
Raster dots, halftone textures and photomechanical collage
Experimental, process-led work that influenced 'New Wave' typography
works: Posters for the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich (late 1970s to 1980s)
Covers for Typografische Monatsblätter (1970s)
The book Typography: My Way to Typography (2000)

title: Sound Masses
idea: Three sirens and colliding sound masses: drag the sirens' pitch planes through space, and where they meet, the masses penetrate or repel.
how: Press PLAY. Each coloured plane is a sound mass driven by a siren (a continuously gliding tone) with a beating cluster around it. Drag the planes up and down (pitch) and left and right (space: pan). When two masses collide, they either penetrate each other (passing through with a burst of your sample, like a percussion crash) or repel (bouncing apart with a thud), depending on REPEL. AUTO keeps them moving. The percussion layer is in the spirit of Ionisation, Varèse's 1931 piece for percussion ensemble with two sirens.

manifesto.name: The Liberation of Sound
manifesto.author: Edgard Varèse
manifesto.where: lectures compiled by Chou Wen-chung and published in Perspectives of New Music (1966)
ideas: Music as 'organised sound', freed from the limits of traditional instruments and the tempered scale.
Sound masses and planes moving in space, colliding, penetrating or repelling each other.
Sirens, percussion and, later, electronics, as in Ionisation (1931) and Poème électronique (1958).
quotes: organized sound
manifesto.system: No notes or scale: continuous sirens and masses that you move through space, and the events come from their collisions, as Varèse described sound masses that penetrate or repel.

design.name: Erik Nitsche
design.who: Erik Nitsche, Swiss-born designer who worked in the United States
hallmarks: Scientific, atomic-age imagery with orbits, diagrams and abstract forms
Bold flat colour planes on dark backgrounds
Modernist sans type with technical precision
works: Atoms for Peace posters for General Dynamics (1955)
General Dynamics corporate design programme (1955 to 1960)
Record covers for Decca (1950s)

title: Constellation
idea: Place a few words on the page like stars: their positions make the rhythm and space, and their letters make the melody.
how: Press PLAY. Each word is a star in a constellation. A slow sweep moves from left to right, and when it reaches a word, the word is sung: each letter is a note (vowels are long and consonants are short, struck with your sample), its height is the pitch register and its size is the loudness. Drag words to move them, double-click the page to add a word (you will be asked for it) and double-click a word to remove it. LAYOUT offers a few starting constellations, including one built on a single word repeated around an empty centre. With a Gemini key, give a theme and Gemini places a new constellation of words.

manifesto.name: From Line to Constellation (vom vers zur konstellation)
manifesto.author: Eugen Gomringer
manifesto.where: published in Switzerland in 1954; Gomringer was then secretary to Max Bill at the Ulm School of Design
ideas: Replace the line of verse with the constellation: a few words grouped on the page, read in any direction.
The poem becomes an object for seeing and using, closer to a sign, a logo or a playful thought game.
Reduction: very few words, with space as active material, as in his poems avenidas (1951) and silencio (1953 to 1954).
manifesto.system: There are no bars or lines. The sweep reads words wherever you place them, so space, size and position on the page are the score, and the letters themselves are the melody.

design.name: Bradbury Thompson
design.who: Bradbury Thompson, American graphic designer and art director
hallmarks: Playful use of letters as images, printed in overlapping process colours (cyan, magenta and yellow)
Bold experiments with type and halftone in printers' magazines
A rational lower-case-only alphabet idea, Alphabet 26
works: Westvaco Inspirations for Printers (1939 to 1962)
Alphabet 26 (1950)
Design for Mademoiselle magazine (1945 to 1959)

title: Letter Drum
idea: A drum machine made of letters: type a line and every character is a percussive phoneme, including Isou's new letters for breaths, clicks, whistles and kisses.
how: Press PLAY. Type into the line (up to 32 characters); each character is one step. Vowels are sung vowel sounds, consonants are percussive (K, T, P and similar are hard hits; S, F, SH and similar are noise; M, N and L are hums), and your sample speaks the capital letters. The extra Lettrist letters in the palette are new sounds: breathing in (↑), breathing out (↓), a click (ʘ), a whistle (~), a kiss (♥), a cough (※) and silence (·). Click them to add them. SCRAMBLE reorders the letters and TEMPO sets the speed.

manifesto.name: Lettrism: Manifesto of Lettrist Poetry
manifesto.author: Isidore Isou
manifesto.where: in Isou's book Introduction à une nouvelle poésie et à une nouvelle musique (Paris, 1947); the Lettrist movement began in Paris in 1945 to 1946
ideas: Poetry reduced beyond words, to letters and their sounds.
An enlarged alphabet of new 'letters' for sounds such as breathing, clicks, whistles and coughs.
A new poetry that merges with music, performed out loud.
manifesto.system: The score is a line of characters. Words are not sung; every letter is a sound in its own right, and Isou's extra sound-letters are part of the alphabet.

design.name: Emigre
design.who: Emigre: Rudy VanderLans and Zuzana Licko, with designers such as Barry Deck
hallmarks: Bitmap and digital typefaces designed for the early Macintosh
Experimental, layered layouts that broke Swiss-style rules
Type designed and published by its users
works: Emigre magazine (1984 to 2005)
Zuzana Licko's bitmap fonts (such as Oakland and Matrix) and Mrs Eaves (1996)
Barry Deck's Template Gothic (1990)

title: Ecstatic Truth
idea: One slider from the accountant's truth to ecstatic truth: the same recording, played plainly as fact or stylised, slowed and staged into something deeper.
how: Press PLAY. Your sample is the 'footage'. With the slider at FACT, it plays exactly as recorded, cut on a strict grid, with a dry log of the facts (times, levels). As you move towards ECSTASY, the machine starts to invent: it slows and stretches the sound, adds a choir drone built from it, reverb, and staged scenes (footsteps in snow, a ship's horn, a far-off bell) that were never in the recording. STAGE A SCENE invents one now. The log changes from facts to stranger, invented captions.

manifesto.name: Minnesota Declaration: Truth and Fact in Documentary Cinema
manifesto.author: Werner Herzog
manifesto.where: read at the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, on 30 April 1999
ideas: Cinéma vérité gives only a superficial 'accountant's truth' of facts.
Deeper truth can be reached only through fabrication, imagination and stylisation.
Ecstatic truth is mysterious and elusive, reached through poetry and invention.
quotes: Fact creates norms, and truth illumination.
There are deeper strata of truth in cinema, and there is such a thing as poetic, ecstatic truth.
manifesto.system: One slider moves between fact and fabrication. At FACT the sample is only documented, but towards ECSTASY the machine stylises and stages it, inventing sounds that were never recorded to reach something truer.

design.name: Saul Bass
design.who: Saul Bass, American graphic designer and film-title designer
hallmarks: Jagged paper cut-out shapes and a single symbolic image
Bold flat colour (often red, black and orange) with hand-cut type
Spirals, fragmented bodies and kinetic title sequences
works: The Man with the Golden Arm titles and poster (1955)
Vertigo titles and poster (1958)
Anatomy of a Murder poster (1959)

title: Both-And
idea: A machine that refuses to choose: every musical decision is a pair of opposites, and in the middle you get both at once. Major and minor, four and three, clean and dirty, straight and swung.
how: Press PLAY. Each of the four big striped sliders is a contradiction. Push it left for one side, right for the other, or leave it in the middle to hear BOTH, which is where Venturi says the life is. HARMONY clashes a major and a minor chord on the same root. METRE runs a four-beat and a three-beat pattern against each other. SURFACE plays your sample clean and distorted. TIME plays straight and swung hats together. MESSY VITALITY adds stray fragments, fills and wrong notes. MORE IS NOT LESS adds another layer each press (a tune, a voice, a texture); a fourth press clears them, because less is a bore. Drop in your own samples: the first is chopped, the second becomes the three-beat hits.

manifesto.name: Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (Nonstraightforward Architecture: A Gentle Manifesto)
manifesto.author: Robert Venturi
manifesto.where: opening chapter of the book, published by the Museum of Modern Art, New York
ideas: Against the 'puritanically moral' purity of orthodox Modern architecture.
Prefer the hybrid, ambiguous and inconsistent: 'both-and' rather than 'either-or'.
A building's richness comes from holding contradictions together, not resolving them away.
quotes: I am for messy vitality over obvious unity.
More is not less.
Blatant simplification means bland architecture. Less is a bore.
manifesto.system: Every control is a contradiction, and none of them make you choose. Each slider blends two opposing layers, and the middle position plays both together, so the music lives in the clash. MESSY VITALITY lets in stray, inconsistent events, and MORE IS NOT LESS keeps piling on layers.

design.name: Supergraphics (Barbara Stauffacher Solomon)
design.who: Barbara Stauffacher Solomon, American designer and landscape architect trained in Basel in Swiss modernism
design.era: San Francisco and The Sea Ranch, California, mid 1960s onwards
hallmarks: Room-sized stripes, circles, arrows and cropped Helvetica letters painted straight onto walls
Flat primary red, blue and yellow with black on white
Graphics that wrap round corners and across ceilings, so the paint changes how the space feels
works: Supergraphics for the Moonraker Athletic Center at The Sea Ranch, California (1966 to 1967)
The Sea Ranch ram's-horn logo
Green Architecture and the Agrarian Garden (book, 1988)

title: Actual Life Journal
idea: A diary you can dance to: a voice memo is chopped into emotional vocal hooks, laid over a field recording and house or two-step garage drums, and taken through intro, build, drop and break.
controls: 6 slots (voice memo, field recording, keys, kick, clap, hats); chop grid with per-step pitch; 3 drum styles with swing; 6 chord progressions in any key; field-bed level and sidechain pump; auto-arranged or hand-played INTRO/BUILD/DROP/BREAK with hold-to-build; Gemini turns a description of your day into an arrangement.
how: Press PLAY: the built-in memo is already chopped and the song starts in its INTRO. Type who said it and the line they said (that becomes the title, like 'Carlos (gotta move on)') and the words flash up as each chop plays. Click the chop grid to choose which piece of the memo plays on each step; the row underneath sets each step's pitch (click up, shift-click down). Hold B (or the BUILD button) for a riser and let go to DROP. Pick HOUSE, 2-STEP or HALF-TIME drums, a chord progression and key. Open the DECK (D) to load your own voice memo, field recording, keys and drums into the slots.
try: Record a 20 second voice memo of a friend telling you about their week. Load it into slot 1, set CHOPS to ONSETS so every word becomes a chop, and build a hook from the three words you like best.
Put a field recording from your street, a pub or a train into slot 2 and push FIELD up during the BREAK. Then pull the slot's FILTER down so it sounds like the room next door to the club.

Load a single held piano or pad note from your Splice folder into slot 3. Set its PITCH so it matches the key, choose vi-IV-I-V and STABS, and play the memo chromatically from a MIDI keyboard over it.

manifesto.name: What would Fred again.. do? The Actual Life method
manifesto.author: Fred again.. (Fred Gibson, b. 1993, London)
manifesto.where: the Actual Life trilogy: Actual Life (April 14 - December 17 2020), Actual Life 2 (February 2 - October 15 2021) and Actual Life 3 (January 1 - September 9 2022)
ideas: Each album is a dated diary. The titles are date ranges, and the songs are built from what was recorded during them.
The samples are real life: voice notes from friends, videos he filmed on nights out, and clips from Instagram and elsewhere, used with permission.
The first person he sampled was Carlos, a construction worker he met in Atlanta. Hungover the next morning, he played piano on his laptop keyboard over what Carlos had said.
Songs are named after the person and their line, like 'Marea (we've lost dancing)', built from a monologue by the DJ The Blessed Madonna.
When a sample can't say exactly what he feels, he writes lyrics and sings on top. The emotion sits over house, garage and breakbeat drums, and builds to euphoric drops.
quotes: I want the music to feel like a collaborative diary
Fred again.., Rolling Stone UK
I want to carry on sampling the world.
Fred again.., NME, 2021
taking these seemingly quite mundane life moments and shining a light on all the beauty that is in those moments
Fred again.., NPR, November 2022
manifesto.system: Slot 1 is the voice memo. It's cut into chops, at its natural word onsets or equally, and a step grid turns them into a hook, with each step pitched inside the key so speech starts to sing. The name and the line give the song its title, and the words flash up with each chop. Under the voice sit a field recording (slot 2), emotional chord progressions played on any sample (slot 3) and a choice of four-to-the-floor house, two-step garage or half-time drums. The arranger moves the song through INTRO (muffled, as if heard from the next room), BUILD (rising filter, snare roll and faster chops), a silent beat before the DROP, and a BREAK. You can let it run or perform it by hand.

design.name: Tibor Kalman and M&Co
design.who: Tibor Kalman (1949 to 1999), Hungarian-born American designer, founder of M&Co in New York and editor of Benetton's Colors magazine
hallmarks: Vernacular type: the lettering of shop signs, menus and typewriters, used on purpose instead of 'good taste'. Here it's the Courier journal.
Huge words that fill the frame one at a time, as in the lyric video M&Co made for Talking Heads' '(Nothing But) Flowers'. Here each chop's word fills the screen.
Colors magazine's direct, image-first layouts with blunt captions, bold red and black, and serious ideas presented with wit.
works: Talking Heads, '(Nothing But) Flowers' lyric video (1988)
Colors magazine, Benetton (Kalman was editor-in-chief, 1990 to 1995)
Tibor Kalman: Perverse Optimist (book, 1998)

title: Seed Garden
idea: Plant sounds as tape loops of different lengths and let them drift in and out of phase, so the music is never the same twice. Garden it with seeds, pruning, weather, a deck of Oblique Strategies and a tape machine that prints the garden back into itself.
controls: 6 slots (piano, voice, texture, bell, found sound, TAPE); up to 12 loop beds, each with its own length, note, sound, swell and pan; scale, key, octave and loop-length programme; attention slider (ignorable to interesting); growth and weather; Discreet-style tape echo with wow and hiss; Oblique Strategies cards that really change the system; PRINT TO TAPE resampling; a Gerstner morphological box that writes a whole programme.
how: Press PLAY. Each ring is a tape loop: the dot goes round once per loop and plays its note when it passes the top. Because no two loops are the same length, they line up differently every time. SEED plants a new loop (S), PRUNE removes one (P) and clicking a ring removes that loop. Turn GROWTH up and the garden seeds and prunes itself, while WEATHER slowly bends the lengths and notes. DRAW A CARD (O) turns over an Oblique Strategy and does what it says to the music. PRINT TO TAPE (T) records the last bars into the TAPE slot and plants it back at half speed. In the PROGRAMME box, click one cell per row or press RANDOM PROGRAMME, then PLANT PROGRAMME to start a new garden from it.
try: Load three single notes from your Splice folder (a piano, a voice 'ooh' and a pad) into slots 1 to 3, set each slot's PITCH so it reads as C, then plant a programme in a pentatonic scale. Every loop will sit in key.

Put a long field recording or a crackly vinyl loop into FOUND SOUND, set its slot START and END to a short, quiet section, and seed it a few times. ATTENTION near 'ignorable' turns it into background weather.
Play for two minutes, PRINT TO TAPE, then PRUNE everything except the tape loop. Seed again around it. Eno's studio idea is that the recording becomes the next instrument.

manifesto.name: What would Brian Eno do? Generative music, tape loops and gardening
manifesto.author: Brian Eno (b. 1948), with Peter Schmidt for Oblique Strategies
manifesto.where: Discreet Music (1975), Oblique Strategies (1975), Music for Airports (1978), 'The Studio as Compositional Tool' (lecture, 1979), Generative Music 1 (1996), 'Composers as Gardeners' (Edge, 2011)
ideas: Set up a system and let it make the music. On Music for Airports, loops of different lengths drift in and out of phase, so the same few notes keep making new combinations.
Discreet Music came from a simple tape-echo system: two tape recorders let a short phrase repeat and decay while he barely touched it.
Oblique Strategies, a deck of cards made with the painter Peter Schmidt, offers one instruction to break a creative deadlock.
The studio is an instrument. A recording can be treated, slowed, layered and fed back in, rather than just capturing a performance.
The composer as gardener: plant seeds and wait to see what comes up, instead of drawing the whole building in advance like an architect.
quotes: as ignorable as it is interesting
Brian Eno, liner notes to Ambient 1: Music for Airports, 1978
someone who plants seeds and waits to see exactly what will come up
Brian Eno on the gardener, 'Composers as Gardeners', Edge, 2011
Honor thy error as a hidden intention
Oblique Strategies, Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt, 1975
manifesto.system: Every planted sound is a loop with its own length, and lengths are chosen to avoid simple ratios, so the pattern doesn't repeat. You don't write a melody; you choose a scale, a few sounds and a range of lengths, then garden. Growth seeds and prunes on its own, and weather bends lengths and notes very slowly. The attention slider moves between music you can ignore (sparse, dark, long swells) and music that rewards listening (brighter, denser, more detail). Each Oblique Strategies card is wired to a real change, and PRINT TO TAPE feeds the garden's own output back in as a new, slower loop.

design.name: Karl Gerstner, Designing Programmes
design.who: Karl Gerstner (1930 to 2017), Swiss designer, painter and co-founder of the agency GGK in Basel
hallmarks: Design as a programme, not a single solution: a set of rules that produces many results. His line 'Instead of solutions for problems, programmes for solutions' fits Eno's systems closely.
The morphological box: a grid of parameters and options, where one path through it gives one design. The PROGRAMME box here works the same way.
Strict sans-serif typography on a flexible grid, and systematic colour arranged in circles and rings, as in his colour paintings.
works: Designing Programmes (book, 1964)
The mobile grid for Capital magazine (1962)
The Forms of Color (book, 1986)

title: Gradual Process
idea: Set a process going and listen to it run: copies of one pattern drift out of phase (Piano Phase, It's Gonna Rain), fill in note by note (Drumming) or stretch out (Four Organs), and new patterns appear from the gaps.
controls: 4 slots (two keyboard voices, a tape loop and a pulse); 4 processes (phase, tape phase, additive build, augmentation); 2 to 4 voices with their own slot, octave and pan; editable 4 to 16 step pattern on a scale grid in any key; continuous or step-wise phasing with drift and hold; build and augmentation rates; chain processes; MIDI transposes.
how: Press PLAY. Two copies of the pattern from Reich's Piano Phase start in unison, and the second one creeps ahead until it has moved a full step, then another, until it comes back to unison. The stripes show how far each voice has moved. Choose a PROCESS: PHASE (notes), TAPE PHASE (two copies of a sample loop at nearly the same speed, like It's Gonna Rain), ADDITIVE (notes appear one at a time in place of rests, like Drumming) or AUGMENTATION (a chord whose notes get longer and longer, like Four Organs). Edit the pattern on the grid (click a cell to set that step's note, click again for a rest). HOLD (H) freezes the drift; ← and → nudge voice 2 by a step; U returns everything to unison.
try: Load one spoken phrase, three or four seconds long, into the TAPE LOOP slot, trim START and END to a single phrase, pick TAPE PHASE and set DRIFT very low. Reich's It's Gonna Rain began with a preacher recorded in Union Square in 1964.

Put a short marimba, kalimba or pluck one-shot from your Splice folder into KEYS A and KEYS B, set both slots' PITCH so the note reads as E, and run PHASE with three voices panned left, centre and right.
Load a clap or shaker into PULSE and choose ADDITIVE with CHAIN on. The pattern builds itself one beat at a time, then the second voice starts to phase, as in Drumming.

manifesto.name: Music as a Gradual Process
manifesto.author: Steve Reich (b. 1936)
manifesto.where: essay first published in the catalogue 'Anti-Illusion: Procedures/Materials', Whitney Museum, New York, 1969, and collected in Reich's Writings on Music
ideas: Music can be a process you can hear happening, not a hidden compositional system.
Once the process is set up, it runs on its own. The composer chooses it, and then the music happens.
The process should be slow and gradual enough that you can follow every detail of it changing.

Phasing: two identical patterns, one a little faster, drift apart and back together. Reich found it by accident with two tape loops of the same phrase (It's Gonna Rain, 1965) and then played it on pianos (Piano Phase, 1967).

Resulting patterns: as the copies overlap, the ear hears new melodies that nobody plays. Drumming (1970 to 1971) also builds patterns by substituting beats for rests, and Four Organs (1970) lengthens the notes of one chord.
quotes: I am interested in perceptible processes.
Steve Reich, 'Music as a Gradual Process', 1968
Once the process is set up and loaded it runs by itself.
Steve Reich, 'Music as a Gradual Process', 1968
turning over an hour glass and watching the sand slowly run through to the bottom
Steve Reich, 'Music as a Gradual Process', 1968
manifesto.system: Voice 1 holds still. In PHASE, each other voice runs a fraction faster, either all the time or in short moves between held positions, until it's one step ahead, and the stripes show the offset. When a voice has moved round a whole pattern, the process is complete and starts again, or moves on to the next process if CHAIN is on. TAPE PHASE does the same with continuous sample loops. ADDITIVE starts each voice with one note and adds one more every few bars. AUGMENTATION stretches each note of a chord a little more every bar. You set the process and its rate, and then listen to it run.

design.name: Anton Stankowski
design.who: Anton Stankowski (1906 to 1998), German graphic designer, photographer and painter, trained in the Folkwang school in Essen and worked in Zurich and Stuttgart
hallmarks: Making invisible processes visible: diagrams that turn forces, flows and systems into lines and fields. Here the phase offset is drawn as stripes.
Rhythmic diagonals and stepped bands of flat colour (blue, red, yellow, black) on white
Constructive, grid-based layouts with plain sans-serif type and no decoration
works: The Deutsche Bank logo, the 'slash in a square' (1974)
The Berlin city corporate design and signage (from 1968)
Look up the Stankowski Stiftung, Stuttgart, for his diagrams and paintings

title: Murmuration
idea: No bird leads a murmuration. Each one follows three local rules and watches about seven neighbours, and the shape of the whole flock comes out of that. Here each bird is also a sound: its height sets the pitch, its heading picks the point in your sample, and its speed sets the level.
controls: 4 species slots (chatter, wings, wind and call) with a mix for each; flock size; Reynolds's separation, alignment and cohesion; topological (k nearest) or metric neighbours; speed, wander and wind; a predator under the mouse with strength; grain rate, length, scale, key and range; wing-wash level; MIDI notes release a flock in that key.
how: Press PLAY. Up to 400 starlings fly by Craig Reynolds's three rules, and each one can trigger a short grain of sound. Move the mouse into the flock: it's a peregrine, and the birds swerve away as a wave (hold the mouse button to dive). Raise ALIGNMENT and the flock moves as one, so the sound becomes a stream. Raise SEPARATION and it scatters into a crackle. Switch NEIGHBOURS between 'k nearest' (what Ballerini and colleagues measured in real starlings) and 'radius' and listen to the flock hold together or break apart. Load your own sounds into the four species slots and set how many birds each one has.
try: Load a long field recording, a minute of rain or a crowd, into CHATTER. Each bird's heading reads from a different point in the file, so the flock scrubs through it as it turns.

Put a single sung note from your Splice folder into CALL, set SCALE to penta (pentatonic) and RANGE to 2 octaves, then sweep ALIGNMENT from 0 to 1. Disorder gives chords, and order makes the flock sing in unison.
Turn the PREDATOR up and hold the mouse down in the middle of the flock. The escape wave runs through the birds like a wave in water, and through your sample.

manifesto.name: Emergence: the murmuration
manifesto.author: Craig Reynolds (1987); Ballerini, Cabibbo, Parisi and colleagues, STARFLAG (2008)
manifesto.where: Reynolds, 'Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model', SIGGRAPH 1987; Ballerini et al., 'Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance', PNAS 105(4), 2008
ideas: Emergence: complex group behaviour can come from simple local rules, with no leader and no plan.
Reynolds's three rules, in order of priority: Collision Avoidance (don't crash), Velocity Matching (fly like your neighbours) and Flock Centering (stay close to them).
Starlings in Rome were filmed in 3D by the STARFLAG team. Each bird follows a fixed number of neighbours, not every bird within a fixed distance, so the flock stays together when it thins out.
A murmuration has no centre, yet it reacts as a whole. A turn spreads through the flock faster than any single bird could signal it.
A musical question: what if each player only listened to the players nearest them?
quotes: the birds choose their own course
Craig Reynolds, 'Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model', 1987
The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is the result of the dense interaction of the relatively simple behaviors of the individual simulated birds.
Craig Reynolds, 1987 (abstract)
each bird interacts on average with a fixed number of neighbors (six–seven), rather than with all neighbors within a fixed metric distance
Ballerini et al., PNAS, 2008 (abstract)
manifesto.system: Each bird looks at its k nearest neighbours (or every bird within a radius). It steers away from any that are too close, turns towards their average heading, and moves towards their centre, with wander, a wind and the predator added. Sound is a grain cloud: every grain is one bird. Its species picks the slot, its height picks a scale degree, its heading picks the point in the sample, its x position sets the pan, its speed sets the level and its depth sets the reverb. Wing-wash is a looped bed whose level follows how fast and how ordered the flock is.

design.name: Muriel Cooper
design.who: Muriel Cooper (1925 to 1994), first design director of the MIT Press, co-founder of the Visible Language Workshop and founding faculty member of the MIT Media Lab
hallmarks: Information Landscapes: translucent, layered type floating in a deep, zoomable 3D space
Seven vertical bars, the MIT Press colophon, abstract book spines spelling 'mitp'
Overlapping translucent colour and the computer used as a design medium, not just a production tool
works: The MIT Press colophon (1964, in use from 1965), now in MoMA's collection
Bauhaus by Hans M. Wingler (MIT Press, 1969)
Information Landscapes, with David Small and others at the Visible Language Workshop, presented at TED5 (1994)

title: The Colour Keyboard
idea: Kandinsky said colour is a keyboard and the soul is the piano. Paint a composition from points, lines, triangles, squares and circles, and a playhead plays it: the colour picks the instrument (yellow is a trumpet, blue a cello), the shape sets how each note is played, and white and black are two kinds of silence.
controls: 6 colour slots (yellow, red, blue, green, orange, violet) for your own sounds; 5 shapes (point, line glissando, triangle, square, circle); size, height and rotation; white (a pause) and black (cuts everything); loop length, tempo, scale, key and range; snap to grid; scan or radial reading; undo and clear; a COMPOSE generator; Gemini paints a composition from a mood; MIDI plays the colours live.
how: Press PLAY. A black bar reads the canvas from left to right. Every shape it crosses sounds: the colour sets the instrument, the height sets the pitch, the size sets how loud and how long, and the shape sets the articulation. A triangle is sharp, high and short, a square is steady and held, a circle swells in slowly and low, a point is a single pluck, and a line slides from one pitch to another. Pick a colour (1 to 8) and a shape (Q point, W line, E triangle, T square, Y circle), then click and drag on the canvas to place it. Shift-click removes a shape. WHITE pauses everything for a moment. BLACK cuts every sound. Press C to COMPOSE a new picture, or describe a mood to Gemini.
try: Load a muted trumpet or brass stab from your Splice folder into YELLOW and a felt-piano note into BLUE. Paint yellow triangles along the top and big blue circles along the bottom, and you have Kandinsky's 'shrill trumpet-note' over his 'darker blue a cello'.
Load your own drum loop into RED, then draw one long red square across the whole loop. Squares hold and loop the sound, so it becomes a bed you can chop with black points.
Ask Gemini for 'Composition VIII, but at 3am in the rain', then shift-click away half of what it paints and see what's left.

manifesto.name: Concerning the Spiritual in Art
manifesto.author: Wassily Kandinsky (1866 to 1944)
manifesto.where: Über das Geistige in der Kunst, Munich, December 1911 (dated 1912). English translation by Michael T. H. Sadler (Sadleir), 1914. Followed by Point and Line to Plane (Bauhaus book, 1926).
ideas: Art should express 'inner necessity', the inner sound of forms and colours, not copy the look of things.

Colours have sounds. Yellow is a shrill trumpet. Light blue is a flute, darker blue a cello, darker still a double bass, and the darkest blue an organ. Green is the placid middle notes of a violin. Orange is the Angelus bell or an old violin. Violet is a cor anglais or a bassoon.

Forms have sounds too. Acute shapes such as the triangle go with sharp colours such as yellow, and deep round shapes such as the circle go with blue. In his Bauhaus questionnaire of 1923 he asked students to pair the yellow triangle, the red square and the blue circle.
White is a silence full of possibility, like a pause in music. Black is the silence of death.
Point and Line to Plane (1926): the point is the smallest element and the line is a point set in motion. Here, points pluck and lines glide.
quotes: Colour is the keyboard, the eyes are the hammers, the soul is the piano with many strings. The artist is the hand which plays, touching one key or another, to cause vibrations in the soul.
Wassily Kandinsky, Concerning the Spiritual in Art, 1911 (trans. Sadler)
Keen lemon-yellow hurts the eye in time as a prolonged and shrill trumpet-note the ear
Kandinsky, 1911
White, therefore, has this harmony of silence, which works upon us negatively, like many pauses in music that break temporarily the melody.
Kandinsky, 1911
The silence of black is the silence of death.
Kandinsky, 1911
manifesto.system: The canvas is a score. Each shape has a colour, a shape, x (when), y (pitch), size (level and length) and rotation (stereo). Colour picks the slot, Kandinsky's instrument. Shape picks the articulation: a point plucks, a line glides from its start pitch to its end pitch, a triangle is sharp and an octave up, a square holds and loops the sound, and a circle swells in an octave down with more reverb. White ducks the whole mix for a pause, and black stops every sound that is playing. In RADIAL mode the bar sweeps like a clock hand from the centre.

design.name: Paul Rand
design.who: Paul Rand (1914 to 1996), American graphic designer, author of Thoughts on Design (1947), designer of the IBM, Westinghouse, ABC and UPS identities, and teacher at Yale
hallmarks: Playful, simple geometry: cut-paper shapes with a hand-made edge, a little crooked, never mechanical
Flat primary colours and lots of white space, often with handwriting next to clean type
Wit and visual puns, like the rebus in the Eye-Bee-M poster (1981)
works: IBM striped logo (1972)
Westinghouse (1960) and ABC (1962) logos
Sparkle and Spin, a children's book with Ann Rand (1957)

title: Live Live
idea: Play a whole set from one pad sampler, the way Fred again.. did at Boiler Room London in 2022: sixteen pads in four banks (one phrase chopped or re-pitched into a melody, drums, chords, effects), a pattern recorder to build the track live from scratch, a CDJ deck underneath, and a held build that drops after a beat of silence.
controls: 7 slots (phrase, keys, kick, clap, hats, CDJ track, field); 4 banks of 16 pads with per-pad pitch, gain, length and pan; phrase chopped at word onsets or equally, or one chop re-pitched across the pads in any key and scale; choke; note repeat (1/8, 1/16, 1/32); quantised overdub pattern recorder (1, 2 or 4 bars) with an editable roll; 4 grooves (house, UK garage 2-step, breakbeat, half-time) with swing and sidechain pump; CDJ deck that locks a loop to tempo, with stop and tape stop; hold-to-build with snare roll, riser and high-pass, gap and drop; FROM SCRATCH autopilot that adds layers in order; MIDI pads on notes 36 to 51.
how: Press PLAY: a groove is already recorded, so you hear chops, chords and drums straight away. Hit the pads with the mouse or the keys 1 2 3 4 / Q W E T / A S F G / Z X C V. [ and ] (or the tabs) switch bank: A VOX CHOPS, B DRUMS, C CHORDS, D FX + PERFORM. Press K to arm the pattern recorder: whatever you play is quantised into the loop, and you can click the roll underneath to add or remove hits. Hold N while holding a pad for note repeat. Hold B (or the BUILD button) for a build, and let go: one beat of silence, then the drop. J starts and stops the CDJ deck. Turn on FROM SCRATCH and the set builds itself up layer by layer, drone first. Open the DECK (D) for your own phrase, drums, keys, a track for the CDJ and a field recording.
try: Record yourself (or a friend, with permission) saying one sentence on your phone, load it into PHRASE, set PADS to ONE CHOP, RE-PITCHED and choose the chop with the best vowel. Now the sixteen pads play that one sound as a melody in key, which is how a single line becomes a whole track.

Load a full loop or track from your Splice folder into the CDJ slot, set CDJ BARS to its length so it locks to the tempo and press J. Finger-drum bank B over it, then press J again to stop it and keep the room going on the pads alone.

Clear every bank (Backspace on each), arm the recorder with K and build the track from nothing, one bank at a time: chords first, then the voice, then hats, kick and clap. Hold B for four bars and let go for the drop.

manifesto.name: What would Fred again.. do? Play it live live: the Boiler Room pad set
manifesto.author: Fred again.. (Fred Gibson, b. 1993, London)
manifesto.where: Boiler Room London (broadcast 29 July 2022), played on a Native Instruments Maschine+ with three Pioneer CDJs and a DJM mixer; and his 2022 Apple Music interview with Zane Lowe, where he showed how he plays the set (reported by MusicTech)
ideas: The whole set can come from one pad sampler. He told Zane Lowe he wanted his live show to come from the Maschine, and on Boiler Room every pad he hits fires a vocal, a drum, a chord or an effect over the tracks on the CDJs.
Play a track as if you are making it from scratch. Demonstrating 'I Found You', he started with layers of drones and then brought in re-pitched pieces of its spoken-word sample.
One phrase can carry a song. A spoken or sung line, cut up and re-pitched across the pads, becomes the hook and the melody.

Tension and release: filters, rolls and risers build up, a moment of silence holds it, and the drop lets it go. The Boiler Room set is remembered for these moments, and for him keeping the room moving when a dancer accidentally pressed stop on a CDJ.
Electronic music played live, not just pressed play on. Fingers on pads, mistakes and all.
quotes: You can play anything on it, like, it's so infinitely powerful
Fred again.. on the Maschine+, Apple Music with Zane Lowe, 2022 (as reported by MusicTech)
with electronic music, it's often almost impossible to get it 'live live.'
Fred again.., same interview
the whole [set] to come from [the Maschine]
Fred again.., same interview (MusicTech's brackets)
manifesto.system: Four banks of sixteen pads, like a pad sampler. Bank A is your phrase (slot 1), cut into chops at its word onsets or into equal slices, or one chop re-pitched to sixteen notes of the key. Bank B is a drum kit built from the kick, clap and hat slots, with a sub bass. Bank C holds chords in the key, played on the keys slot. Bank D is for performing: risers, impacts, reverse vocals, throws, tape stop, filter moves, a gap, a drop and the CDJ. A quantised pattern recorder loops whatever you play, so a set can start empty and be built in front of people. The CDJ deck locks a loop (slot 6) to the tempo. BUILD automates a high-pass filter, a snare roll and a riser and mutes the kick; on release, the beat stops for one beat and comes back with an impact. FROM SCRATCH adds the layers in order (drone, voice, hats, build, drop, break). Which pad holds which sound in his real set isn't documented: the bank layout here is our interpretation.

design.name: Barney Bubbles
design.who: Barney Bubbles (Colin Fulcher, 1942 to 1983), British designer for Stiff and Radar Records, Hawkwind, Ian Dury and Elvis Costello, who rarely signed his work
hallmarks: Modernism as a toybox: he borrowed from Kandinsky, Russian Constructivism, the Bauhaus and pop art and made it playful. Here the pads are geometric shapes in primary colours.
Many versions of one thing: Ian Dury's 'Do It Yourself' came in many different wallpaper-pattern sleeves. Here each bank has its own pattern and colourway.
Hidden jokes, codes and symbols, tightly condensed type and a lot of nerve. Look for the small marks around the pads.
works: Ian Dury and the Blockheads, 'Do It Yourself' (1979)
Elvis Costello and the Attractions, 'Armed Forces' (1979)
Hawkwind, 'Space Ritual' (1973); and Paul Gorman's book 'Reasons to be Cheerful: The Life and Work of Barney Bubbles' (2008)

title: Endless Music Box
idea: A playable generative instrument after Eno and Peter Chilvers' Bloom (2008): tap and each note blooms, comes back every cycle a little quieter and slowly drifts, and when you stop playing the music box carries on by itself, over a slowly recombining painting of colour fields.
controls: 5 slots (glass, piano, voice, drone, painting texture); 12 moods (key, scale, sounds and colours) with shuffle; cycle length and a second, out-of-step cycle for the right half; decay per repeat or FREEZE; drift (repeats wander to neighbouring notes); chord taps; range and brightness; evolve-when-idle with its own wait and density; drone and painting layers; echo and reverb; MIDI notes plant notes.
how: Press PLAY. Nothing to learn: the box starts playing itself. Click or tap anywhere on the dark field: higher is a higher note, left and right is the stereo position. Each note comes back once every CYCLE and gets quieter each time, so what you play turns into a slowly fading loop. Stop touching it and after a few seconds EVOLVE takes over. M changes MOOD (Shift+M shuffles), X clears the field, F freezes every note so nothing fades, ↑ and ↓ change the cycle, and 1 to 8 plant notes from the keyboard. Turn on TWO CYCLES and notes on the right half repeat on a different cycle, so the two halves drift in and out of step. Open the DECK (D) to swap the glass, piano, voice, drone and texture for your own sounds.
try: Load a single soft note from your Splice folder (a felt piano, a kalimba or a sung 'ooh') into GLASS, set the slot's PITCH so it reads as C, then tap a slow three-note phrase near the top and leave it. The phrase fades over a minute or two while EVOLVE adds to it.

Put a long pad or field recording into DRONE and a texture (rain, vinyl crackle, tape hiss) into PAINTING. Choose a mood, set DECAY high and EVOLVE density low, and leave it on as music you can ignore.

Turn on TWO CYCLES with a ratio near 1.5, play a few notes on the left and a few on the right, then FREEZE. You'll hear the halves line up differently every time, the Music for Airports idea played by hand.

manifesto.name: What would Brian Eno do? Bloom: an endless music machine
manifesto.author: Brian Eno (b. 1948) and Peter Chilvers
manifesto.where: Generative Music 1 (SSEYO Koan, 1996), 77 Million Paintings (2006) and the Bloom app for iPhone (released 5 October 2008), made with the musician and software designer Peter Chilvers
ideas: Generative music: write the rules, not the notes, and the music is different every time you hear it. Eno released Generative Music 1 in 1996 using the SSEYO Koan software.
Bloom is part instrument, part composition, part artwork. Touch the screen and a note plays and blooms into a circle, then repeats at a regular interval, getting softer, until it fades away.
When Bloom is left alone, a generative player takes over and keeps making music and pictures.
Moods change the scale, the sounds and the colours, so the same gesture gives a different piece.
77 Million Paintings applies the same idea to images: layers of Eno's painted slides recombine slowly, so you are unlikely ever to see the same picture twice.
quotes: an endless music machine, a music box for the 21st century. You can play it, and you can watch it play itself.
Brian Eno on Bloom, 2008 (the app's description)
Like live music, it is always different.
Brian Eno on generative music, The Independent, 1996
You mean you used to listen to exactly the same thing over and over again?
Brian Eno, imagining his grandchildren, The Independent, 1996
manifesto.system: Every tap makes a note object with a pitch (height, in the mood's scale), a pan (left to right) and a sound (by height, or the one you pick). The note plays at once and then again every CYCLE seconds, losing a little level each time (DECAY) until it disappears. FREEZE stops the fading. DRIFT lets each repeat wander to a neighbouring note, so a phrase slowly changes. With TWO CYCLES, the right half of the field runs on a different, out-of-step cycle, like the unsynchronised loops of Music for Airports. If you stop for longer than the IDLE time, EVOLVE plays the box itself with a slow random walk. Behind it, a drone holds the key, and the PAINTING layer recombines coloured fields and swells a texture each time, after 77 Million Paintings. Moods here are our own, not Bloom's twelve.

design.name: Vaughan Oliver and v23 (4AD)
design.who: Vaughan Oliver (1957 to 2019), British designer for the record label 4AD, working as 23 Envelope with the photographer Nigel Grierson and later as v23 with Chris Bigg
hallmarks: Atmosphere before information: blurred, close-up, often unidentifiable photography and textures that set a mood. Here the field is dark, grainy and soft-focus.
Elegant type used sparingly and very small, set against huge empty space, with serif italics and widely spaced capitals. Here the captions sit in the corners and run up the side.
Layering: transparent images, scratches and light leaks stacked over each other, so the cover rewards a long look, like ambient music. Here the painting layers stack and slowly change.
works: Cocteau Twins, 'Treasure' (1984)
This Mortal Coil, 'It'll End in Tears' (1984)
Pixies, 'Doolittle' (1989); and Rick Poynor's book 'Vaughan Oliver: Visceral Pleasures' (2000)

title: Closed Groove
idea: Pierre Schaeffer's musique concrète as a four-turntable instrument: cut any sound into eight sound objects, label each one with a simplified version of his typology, then loop them in closed grooves, slow them down, cut off their attacks and reverse them, the way the Étude aux chemins de fer was made from railway recordings in 1948.
controls: 4 source slots (railway, bell, voice, tone) cut into 4 to 8 objects at onsets or equally; per-turntable source, object, hit or closed-groove mode, speed, attack cut, length, reverse, level, pan, tone, space and a 16-step pattern; tempo and swing; acousmatic (reduced listening) mode; automatic étude; spatial relief.
how: Press PLAY: four turntables (the wheels) play objects cut from a built-in railway recording and a bell. Click an object in the strip (A to H) to hear it and give it to the selected turntable, or press 1 to 8. Click the step grid on a turntable to change its rhythm. Set a turntable to CLOSED GROOVE and its object loops forever, the steps opening and closing it. Raise ATTACK CUT on the bell to hear Schaeffer's 'cut bell'. Tab picks the next turntable, G toggles closed groove, V reverses, ↑ ↓ change its speed, A switches on acousmatic listening (sources hidden), U starts the automatic étude. Load your own sounds into the four sources (D opens the deck).
try: Load one Splice one-shot you know well (a vocal 'hey', a snare, a door) into SOURCE A, switch on ACOUSMATIC and listen to its eight objects without knowing which is which. Describe each one only by its shape (attack, body, decay), which is reduced listening.

Put a piano or bell note into SOURCE B, set a turntable to CLOSED GROOVE on object A, then raise ATTACK CUT. With the strike gone, the tail becomes a new instrument, as Schaeffer found with his cut bell.

Record four seconds of your own street, kitchen or train journey on your phone, load it into SOURCE A, set objects to 8 at onsets and switch on the AUTOMATIC ÉTUDE. That's your own étude aux chemins de fer.

manifesto.name: Pierre Schaeffer: musique concrète and the sound object
manifesto.author: Pierre Schaeffer (1910 to 1995), with Pierre Henry and the Groupe de Recherche de Musique Concrète
manifesto.where: Studio d'Essai of French radio, Paris. The Étude aux chemins de fer (railway study) was broadcast in the 'Concert de bruits' on 5 October 1948. The theory was set out in 'Traité des objets musicaux' (1966).
ideas: Musique concrète starts from recorded sounds rather than notes on paper. The composer works directly on the 'concrete' material and finds the structure by listening.
The 1948 études were made with discs. A 'sillon fermé' (closed groove) cut into the disc locked a fragment into an endless loop, about forty years before the sampler.
The 'cloche coupée' (cut bell): remove the attack from a bell and what you hear is no longer a bell. The identity of a sound lives a lot in its first moments.
Reduced listening (écoute réduite) means listening to a sound for its own qualities (shape, grain, mass, how it moves), not for its cause or its meaning.

The sound object (objet sonore) is what you hear when you listen that way. Schaeffer sorted objects with a typology, for example sustained against impulse against iterative, and tonic (with a pitch) against complex. The labels here simplify it.
Acousmatic listening means hearing a sound without seeing its source, as Pythagoras' students were said to hear him from behind a curtain. Radio and loudspeakers made this normal.
quotes: For years, we often did phenomenology without knowing it
Pierre Schaeffer, Traité des objets musicaux (1966), in Brian Kane's translation
a sound that one hears without seeing the causes behind it
Schaeffer's Traité (1966) quoting a dictionary definition of 'acousmatic'. This is a translation and the wording varies, so treat it as a paraphrase.
Deprived of its percussion, the bell becomes an oboe sound
Schaeffer on the cut bell, in English translation. The wording varies between sources.
manifesto.system: Each source slot is analysed when it loads. Its region (start to end, reversed if set) is cut into OBJECTS at detected onsets, or into equal parts, giving objects A to H. Each object gets a simplified Schaeffer-style label from its loudness envelope and periodicity: N = tonic (clear pitch), X = complex (noisy), ' = impulse (short), " = iterative (repeated pulses), and no mark = sustained. Four turntables each play one object. In HIT mode it is retriggered on the active steps of the turntable's 16-step pattern. In CLOSED GROOVE mode it loops continuously and the steps open and close a gate. SPEED changes pitch and duration together, like changing disc speed. ATTACK CUT skips the first milliseconds and fades in, which is the cut bell. RELIEF slowly moves the turntables around the stereo field, after the 'pupitre d'espace' (the spatialisation desk Schaeffer's studio built in 1951). The AUTOMATIC ÉTUDE changes one thing every two bars.

design.name: A. M. Cassandre
design.who: A. M. Cassandre (Adolphe Jean-Marie Mouron, 1901 to 1968), Ukrainian-born French poster artist and type designer
hallmarks: Geometry and huge scale: a locomotive, a ship's bow or a pair of rails reduced to bold shapes, often seen from very low down or converging to one vanishing point.
Airbrushed gradients and a limited palette of navy, black, cream and red, with light that glows like a lamp in fog.

Lettering built as part of the picture, often in his own display faces Bifur (1929) and Peignot (1937), with wide geometric capitals set along an edge. Here the turntables are drawn as locomotive wheels.
works: Étoile du Nord (1927), rails converging to a star
Nord Express (1927), the locomotive as a wedge of speed
Normandie (1935), the ocean liner's bow towering over the viewer; and Dubonnet (1932), the drinker filled in panel by panel

title: Golden Angle
idea: A sunflower head as a sequencer: seeds are born one by one, each turned 137.5° from the last (the golden angle), as in H. Vogel's 1979 model of phyllotaxis. Every birth is a note, a rotating arm plays the seeds it passes, and a Fibonacci-word rhythm ticks underneath. Change the angle and you can hear (and see) why plants pick the irrational one.
controls: 5 slots (seed, petal, bell, drone, pulse); divergence angle with golden, Lucas and rational presets; birth rate, maximum seeds and what happens when the head is full; 1, 2, 3 or 5 arms, sweep speed, listening band and quantise; pitch from spiral family (n mod 8, 13, 21 or 34) or from radius; key, scale and octaves; Fibonacci-word rhythm of length 8, 13, 21 or 34; spiral overlay; drone, swing and space.
how: Press PLAY: a seed is born every eighth note, 137.5° round from the last. Its pitch comes from which spiral it belongs to, and the angle sets its stereo position. The black arm sweeps round and plays any seed inside the dashed LISTENING BAND. Drag the ANGLE slider (or ← →) away from 137.5° and watch the even sunflower break into straight spokes: the sweep then plays in lumpy bursts. G snaps back to golden. 1, 2, 3 and 5 set the number of arms, F changes the spiral family used for pitch, S shows the spirals, W toggles the Fibonacci-word rhythm, Q quantise and N starts a new head. Load your own sounds into the deck (D): SEED plays most notes.
try: Load a soft mallet or kalimba one-shot from Splice into SEED and a plucked string into PETAL, set PITCH FROM to 'spiral 13' with a pentatonic scale. Every 13th seed lands on the same note, so you hear the spirals as a slow melody.

Set the angle to exactly 180°, then 120°, 90° and 137.3°, listening to the sweep each time. Rational angles make spokes and bursts. 137.508° spreads seeds most evenly, which is why it packs a sunflower best.
Put a short percussive sample into PULSE, turn the Fibonacci word to 13 against the 16-step bar and swing up to 0.2. You get a never-quite-repeating groove from the rule 'a → ab, b → a'.

manifesto.name: Phyllotaxis: the golden angle and the sunflower
manifesto.author: H. Vogel; Stéphane Douady and Yves Couder; Alan Turing; D'Arcy Thompson
manifesto.where: D'Arcy Thompson, 'On Growth and Form' (1917); Alan Turing's unfinished 'Morphogen theory of phyllotaxis' (early 1950s, published after his death); H. Vogel, 'A better way to construct the sunflower head', Mathematical Biosciences (1979); S. Douady and Y. Couder, 'Phyllotaxis as a physical self-organized growth process', Physical Review Letters (1992)
ideas: Phyllotaxis means 'leaf arrangement'. Leaves, florets and seeds are laid down one at a time at the growing tip, each turned by roughly the same divergence angle from the last.

In many plants that angle is close to 137.5°, the golden angle: 360° divided by the golden ratio squared. Because it is the 'most irrational' angle, no two seeds ever line up into a spoke, so they pack evenly at every size.
Vogel's model puts seed n at angle n × 137.508° and radius c√n. That one rule produces the sunflower's crossing spirals, whose counts are neighbouring Fibonacci numbers (for example 34 and 55).

Douady and Couder showed in 1992 that the pattern appears from physics alone. Drops of magnetised fluid falling on oil repel each other and settle into Fibonacci spirals, so nothing needs to 'know' the golden ratio.
Philosophically, form is a record of growth: the pattern is what is left behind by a simple process repeated in time, which is also a fair description of a piece of music.
quotes: Cell and tissue, shell and bone, leaf and flower, are so many portions of matter, and it is in obedience to the laws of physics that their particles have been moved, moulded and conformed.
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1917)
A better way to construct the sunflower head
the title of H. Vogel's paper, Mathematical Biosciences 44 (1979), which gave θ = n × 137.508°, r = c√n
Phyllotaxis as a physical self-organized growth process
the title of Douady and Couder's paper, Physical Review Letters 68 (1992)
manifesto.system: Seed n is placed at angle n × ANGLE and radius √n (Vogel's model). A new seed is BORN every BIRTH steps and plays at once. Its pan is set by its angle, and its pitch by its spiral family (n mod F, mapped onto the scale) or by its radius. Its sound follows the Fibonacci word: 'a' seeds use SEED (about 62%), 'b' seeds use PETAL, and every F-th seed rings the BELL. One to five ARMS rotate once every SWEEP bars and replay any seed inside the LISTENING BAND as they pass it, either at its exact angle or quantised to the 16th-note grid. The PULSE track plays the first L letters of the Fibonacci word (a = hit, b = rest) as a looping rhythm, which goes in and out of phase with the 16-step bar. When the head is full it restarts, holds, or wilts (the oldest seeds drop out). The readout shows the two visible spiral counts, found from the newest seed's nearest neighbours.

design.name: Max Huber
design.who: Max Huber (1919 to 1992), Swiss graphic designer trained in Zurich who worked mainly in Milan, for Studio Boggeri, La Rinascente, Einaudi and the Monza racetrack
hallmarks: Overlapping transparent shapes in printing primaries (red, yellow, blue and black on white) that mix where they cross, like overprinted inks. Here the seeds overlap and multiply.
Motion and rotation shown with spirals, speed lines and swirling bands of colour. Here the sweep arm and birth rings.
Bold, clean sans-serif type and numbers used as images, in strong asymmetric layouts influenced by Swiss modernism and Max Bill. Here the angle itself is the headline.
works: Gran Premio dell'Autodromo di Monza posters (from 1948)
La Rinascente logo (1950)
Book covers for the publisher Einaudi (1940s and 1950s)

title: Rayonist Rays
idea: Larionov and Goncharova's Rayonist manifesto made playable: objects send out coloured rays, which reflect off the edges, and music happens only where rays cross. A scan line reads the intersections from left to right like a score, so the 'spatial forms arising from the intersection of the reflected rays' are what you hear.
controls: 5 slots (four ray timbres and an object hum); drag, add or delete objects and give each one a timbre, a ray count and a spin; rays, fan spread, length, rotation and edge reflection; 'objects play no role' mode; scan length, notes per step, key, scale and octaves; Futurist motor (kick and hats), swing, echo and space; optional Gemini that turns a scene you describe into objects.
how: Press PLAY. The coloured rays slowly turn, and every white dot where two rays cross is a note: its height is the pitch, and the steeper the crossing, the louder and shorter the note. The black scan line plays the dots as it passes. Drag an object to move it, click empty space to add one, and Shift+click (or Delete) removes the selected one. 1 to 5 set the selected object's timbre, [ and ] change its number of rays. O switches on 'objects play no role' (only the rays remain), E toggles reflection, N makes a new scene and ← → change the scan speed. Describe a scene for Gemini, or leave the key empty and the built-in version picks things from the manifesto's own list.
try: Load four short tonal one-shots from your Splice folder (a synth stab, a glass hit, a sung note, a muted guitar) into RAY A to D, give each object a different one, then move two objects close together. Close objects mean many shallow crossings: long, soft notes.

Switch on OBJECTS PLAY NO ROLE and turn REFLECT on and off. The 'reflected rays' fill the whole canvas with crossings, so the music thickens from the edges in, which is the manifesto's point that the picture is made of rays, not things.

Ask Gemini for 'Moscow tram stop in the rain, 1913' (or press N for a built-in scene), set the Futurist motor to 0.6 and the scan to 1 bar. You get a city symphony where the objects are only the excuse.

manifesto.name: Rayonists and Futurists: A Manifesto
manifesto.author: Mikhail Larionov (1881 to 1964) and Natalia Goncharova (1881 to 1962), signed with other Moscow artists
manifesto.where: Published in the miscellany 'Donkey's Tail and Target' (Oslinyi khvost i mishen), Moscow, 1913. English translation in John E. Bowlt, 'Russian Art of the Avant-Garde: Theory and Criticism 1902 to 1934' (1976).
ideas: Rayonism (luchizm) paints not objects but the rays of light reflected from them, and the new forms made where those rays cross.
The painting should exist for its own sake, with its own laws of colour and line. The objects of everyday life are only a starting point.
The manifesto celebrates the modern city (trousers, jackets, shoes, trolleys, cars, airplanes, railways, grandiose steamships) while turning against Western imitation: 'Long live the beautiful East!'
Rayonism aimed at a kind of fourth dimension: time and movement in a still picture, so painting could flow like music.
Larionov and Goncharova were also stage designers for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, carrying the coloured-ray style into theatre.
quotes: spatial forms arising from the intersection of the reflected rays of various objects, forms chosen by the artist's will
Rayonists and Futurists: A Manifesto (1913), trans. John E. Bowlt
The ray is depicted provisionally on the surface by a colored line.
Rayonists and Futurists: A Manifesto (1913), trans. Bowlt
painting becomes equal to music while remaining itself
Rayonists and Futurists: A Manifesto (1913), trans. Bowlt
manifesto.system: Each object sends out a fan of RAYS that slowly rotate (SPIN). With REFLECT on, a ray that hits the edge bounces once, like light reflected around a room. Every point where two rays from different objects cross is a note. Its pitch comes from its height (in the scale), its timbre from the slot of one of the two objects (first, second, or alternating), and its loudness and length from the crossing angle: square crossings are short and loud, glancing ones long and soft. The SCAN line crosses the picture once every SCAN bars and plays the crossings it passes, up to NOTES PER STEP. When objects play a role, the scan also sounds each object itself as a low hum. With OBJECTS PLAY NO ROLE, they disappear from view and sound and only the rays remain. The Futurist MOTOR adds kick and hats.

design.name: Milton Glaser
design.who: Milton Glaser (1929 to 2020), American graphic designer, co-founder of Push Pin Studios (1954, with Seymour Chwast, Reynold Ruffins and Edward Sorel) and of New York magazine (1968, with Clay Felker)
hallmarks: Flat, bright bands of colour against black silhouettes, with curling, rainbow-like forms. Here the rays are flat bands in a psychedelic palette.
Eclectic borrowing from Art Nouveau, Victorian type, comics and Persian miniatures, in reaction to strict Swiss modernism.

Wit and the rebus: a picture standing in for a word (as in I ♥ NY), plus rounded hand-drawn display faces such as Baby Teeth. Here the title is set in a rounded display face and the objects are rebus-like black dots.
works: Bob Dylan poster for Columbia Records' Greatest Hits (1966/67)
I ♥ NY campaign logo (1977)
New York magazine (founded 1968) and the Push Pin Graphic

title: Spoken Mantra
kicker: WHAT WOULD FRED AGAIN.. DO? · FOUND SPEECH
idea: A spoken sentence, not a sung one, becomes the whole song, the way Fred again.. built 'Marea (we've lost dancing)' around The Blessed Madonna's speaking voice. The speech is cut into words, you choose which words make the mantra, a piano listens to the pitch of each word and harmonises it, and the arrangement runs intro, mantra, build (the phrase shrinks to one stuttering word), a beat of silence, then a pumping house or two-step drop.
controls: 6 slots (speech, piano, kick, clap, hats, field recording); click words to build the mantra; word chopping by gaps or equal slices; phrase timing natural or quantised; key, mode and progression or 'follow the speech'; groove (house, two-step, half-time, none), sidechain pump, hook density and re-pitched hooks; section lengths, auto-arrange or play sections by hand with a held build; riser, echo and space; optional Gemini that turns a moment you describe into an arrangement.
how: Press PLAY. The built-in 'speech' is cut into words (the boxes in the SPEECH window). Click a word to take it in or out of the mantra. The piano reads the pitch of each word and picks a chord that contains it. With AUTO on, the song moves through INTRO, MANTRA, BUILD, DROP and BREAK by itself; press 1 to 5 to jump to a section at the next bar, or Enter for the next one. With AUTO off, the build holds on its last stutter until you press Enter, and the drop lands after a beat of silence. Drop a voice memo or any spoken sample onto the page (it goes to the SPEECH slot), or press D for all six slots.
try: Record ten seconds of a friend talking on your phone (a voice note is perfect), drop it in, and switch off every word except the two that hit you. Set CHOP to 'gaps' and PHRASE TIMING to '8ths' so the words land on the grid, then let AUTO run to the drop.

Load a long field recording from your Splice folder (rain, a station, a crowd) into FIELD and a soft felt-piano one-shot recorded at C into PIANO. Set PROGRESSION to 'follow the speech', GROOVE to 'two-step' and PUMP to 0.7: the piano follows your talker's voice and breathes with the kick.

Turn AUTO off, play MANTRA for a while, press 3 for the BUILD and let it hold on the one-word stutter as long as you can bear. Press Enter, listen to the beat of silence, then the drop. Record it with R and use the WAV as a new speech sample.

manifesto.name: What would Fred again.. do? Found speech as the song: the 'Marea (we've lost dancing)' method
manifesto.author: Fred again.. (Fred Gibson, b. 1993, London), with The Blessed Madonna (Marea Stamper)
manifesto.where: 'Marea (we've lost dancing)', Fred again.. and The Blessed Madonna, single released in early 2021 and later on 'Actual Life (April 14 – December 17 2020)'. Also his habit of naming tracks after the person whose voice is in them: 'Kyle (i found you)', 'Delilah (pull me out of this)', 'Billie (loving arms)'.
ideas: The voice in a Fred again.. track is often speaking, not singing: a few words lifted from a conversation, a voice note or a video, repeated until they become a hook. 'Marea (we've lost dancing)' is built around The Blessed Madonna talking about the loss of dancing during the 2020 lockdowns.
The track is named after the person whose voice it uses, with their phrase in brackets. The sample is treated as a portrait of a real person at a real moment.
Repetition changes meaning: a sentence heard once is information; heard sixteen times over chords it becomes a mantra, and then something you can dance to.
The arrangement does the emotional work: a quiet, almost ambient opening with piano, a long build in which the phrase is cut shorter and shorter, and a euphoric drop with a pumping house kick.
He has often said in interviews that he collects these moments constantly on his phone and that the emotional weight of the real voice matters more than polish. (Paraphrase.)
manifesto.system: The SPEECH slot is cut into words, either at the gaps between them (energy below a threshold) or into equal slices. Each word's pitch is estimated by autocorrelation and snapped to the key. You choose which words form the MANTRA. In PROGRESSION 'follow the speech', each bar's chord is a diatonic triad that contains the pitch of that bar's lead word, so the piano harmonises the speaking voice (this is the instrument's interpretation, not a claim about how Fred works). Sections: INTRO (speech, field recording and soft held piano), MANTRA (the phrase every bar, piano on the beat), BUILD (the phrase shrinks: whole phrase, last two words, last word on beats, then 8ths and 16ths, with a riser, rising filter and snare roll; the final beat is silent), DROP (full groove, sidechain pump on piano and field, and re-pitched hooks made of the lead word tuned to the chord), BREAK (no drums, long reverb). AUTO moves through them; without AUTO the build holds until you press Enter.

design.name: Susan Kare
design.who: Susan Kare (b. 1954), American artist and designer, who drew the original icons, bitmap fonts and interface graphics for the Apple Macintosh (1983 to 1986), and later icons for Windows 3.0 and many others
hallmarks: Icons drawn on a grid of square pixels, often 32 × 32, in pure black and white, with enormous character in very few dots. Here every section is a hand-drawn pixel icon (moon, speech balloon, stairs, bomb, cup), and the bomb nods to her system-error icon.
Bitmap typefaces designed for the screen and named after cities (Chicago, Geneva, New York). Here a pixel face stands in for Chicago in the title bars and menus.

The 1-bit desktop: a dithered grey pattern, windows with striped title bars and close boxes, the menu bar across the top. The command-key symbol she adopted (⌘) came from a Swedish sign for a place of interest; it appears in the menu bar here.
works: Original Macintosh icons: the trash can, the watch, the paintbrush, the bomb (1984)
The Chicago, Geneva and Monaco bitmap fonts (1984)
Windows 3.0 Solitaire card deck (1990)

title: Discreet System
kicker: WHAT WOULD BRIAN ENO DO? · DISCREET MUSIC, 1975
idea: Brian Eno's Discreet Music (1975) as an instrument you set going and then leave alone: two short melodies of different lengths feed a graphic equaliser and a long tape-delay loop of two tape machines, so every note comes back, quieter and darker, for minutes. Draw the EQ, let it drift, turn the listening level down to the edge of hearing like the harp record Eno couldn't get up to turn up, and bring in canon players who each slow down at a different rate.
controls: 4 slots (line A, line B, canon players, room tone); two (or three) melodies with their own note counts and lengths, drawn on a grid; key and scale; tape delay time, feedback, wow, tape tone and saturation, a short echo; an 8-band graphic EQ you draw, with optional slow drift; listening level and a one-speaker 'harp record' mode; Pachelbel canon players with tempo spread; tempo and space.
how: Press PLAY and leave it. Line A and line B (the two bars at the bottom) repeat at different lengths, so they line up differently each time. Every note goes into the TAPE loop and comes back after the delay time, a little quieter and duller, which is what the generation chart counts: one symbol per note still circulating on the tape. Click a line's grid to change a note (higher is higher), drag the EQ columns to reshape the sound, F lets the EQ drift by itself. H is the harp record: very quiet, one speaker. V brings in the canon players. ← → change the delay time, ↑ ↓ the feedback, C clears the tape.
try: Load two soft sustained one-shots from your Splice folder recorded at C (a pad note and a breathy synth) into LINE A and LINE B, set the tape to about 8 seconds and feedback to 0.85, and do nothing for five minutes. Then change one note.

Put a long, quiet room tone or rain into ROOM, switch on H (the harp record) and work on something else with this playing. Notice when you notice it: that is the point of ambient music as Eno described it.

Load a short string or vocal phrase into CANON, switch V on, set the players to 4 and the spread to 0.3, and pull the line levels down. The players start together and slowly fall apart, like the B side of Discreet Music.

manifesto.name: What would Brian Eno do? Discreet Music: a system set into operation
manifesto.author: Brian Eno (b. 1948); B side performed by the Cockpit Ensemble, conducted by Gavin Bryars
manifesto.where: 'Discreet Music', Obscure Records no. 3 (1975). The sleeve reproduces Eno's operational diagram of the system and his notes on how the piece came about. See also Fripp and Eno, '(No Pussyfooting)' (1973), for the two-tape-recorder delay system.
ideas: Set up a system, then let it run. The title piece came from two simple melodic lines of different lengths, stored on an EMS synthesiser's digital recall, fed through a graphic equaliser and an echo unit into a long tape-delay loop made of two tape recorders.
The diagram is the score. The sleeve shows the patch, not the notes, because the music is what that arrangement of machines does.
Eno adjusted the timbre only occasionally with the equaliser; the rest of the time the system played itself for about half an hour.

Listening at the edge of hearing: in the sleeve notes he describes lying in bed after an accident with a record of eighteenth-century harp music playing too quietly from one speaker, unable to get up and fix it, and starting to hear it as part of the room, like the light and the rain. (Paraphrase.)

On the B side, the Cockpit Ensemble play three variations on Pachelbel's Canon in D, each built from a simple system applied to the parts, such as changes of tempo between the players (Fullness of Wind, French Catalogues, Brutal Ardour).
quotes: Since I have always preferred making plans to executing them, I have gravitated towards situations and systems that, once set into operation, could create music with little or no intervention on my part.
Brian Eno, sleeve notes to Discreet Music (1975)
manifesto.system: Line A and line B are short loops of notes (scale degrees) with different total lengths in beats, so their alignment keeps changing. They play the LINE slots into an 8-band graphic EQ (peaking filters you draw; DRIFT nudges one band every few seconds, as Eno occasionally turned a knob), then a short echo, then the TAPE: two long delay lines (left and right, the right one about 7% longer, standing in for the two tape machines) whose output is fed back through tape saturation and a low-pass filter, so each pass is quieter and duller. WOW wobbles the tape speed slightly. The generation chart is an Isotype count: one symbol per note on the tape, one row per pass. LISTENING LEVEL and the H 'harp record' mode drop everything to a whisper in one speaker. The CANON players play the Pachelbel bass line (in your key) in different octaves, each at a slightly slower tempo than the last, so they start together and drift apart: the instrument's simplified take on the B side's tempo systems.

design.name: Isotype (Otto Neurath, Marie Neurath and Gerd Arntz)
design.who: Isotype (International System of Typographic Picture Education), developed by the philosopher Otto Neurath (1882 to 1945) with the 'transformer' Marie Reidemeister, later Neurath (1898 to 1986), and the artist Gerd Arntz (1900 to 1988), who cut the pictograms in linocut
design.era: Vienna 1925 to 1934 (as the 'Vienna Method of Pictorial Statistics'), then The Hague and, from 1942, Oxford and London
hallmarks: Count, don't scale: a larger quantity is shown by more identical symbols, never by a bigger symbol. Here every note still on the tape is one symbol, and each pass of the tape is one row.

Flat, simplified pictograms with no perspective, drawn to work at small sizes. Here the synthesiser, the equaliser and the two tape machines are drawn as flat pictograms, as in the Discreet Music diagram.
A restrained palette of flat colours (red, blue, ochre, black) on cream paper, and a geometric sans serif (Futura was the house face; Jost stands in for it here).
works: 'Gesellschaft und Wirtschaft' (Society and Economy), a 100-chart atlas (1930)
Gerd Arntz's pictogram archive (about 4,000 symbols), now online from the Gemeentemuseum Den Haag
Marie Neurath's Isotype children's books, such as 'If You Could See Inside' (1940s and 1950s)

title: Row Matrix
kicker: THEORY OF COMPOSITION · SCHOENBERG'S TWELVE-TONE METHOD, 1923
idea: Arnold Schoenberg's method of composing with twelve tones as a four-voice instrument. One row of all twelve pitch classes is laid out as the full 12 × 12 matrix of its 48 forms (prime, inversion, retrograde, retrograde inversion, at every transposition). Give each voice a form, cut its row into chords, scatter it across octaves and hear the aggregate (all twelve notes) complete, again and again, with no note given priority over another.
controls: 5 slots (four voices plus an aggregate bell); the row itself (swap notes, random row, all-interval row, four famous rows); for each of four voices: form (P, I, R, RI) and transposition, chosen by clicking the matrix, rhythm in 16ths, chord segmentation (single notes, dyads, trichords, tetrachords, hexachords), octave, register spread, rest chance, level and what happens at the end of a row (repeat, mirror, transpose by the row, random form); Klangfarben mode that passes the melody between instruments; a hexachordal combinatoriality finder that pairs voices so their hexachords complete aggregates; tempo, swing, reverb and echo.
how: Press PLAY. Voice 1 (red) plays the row's prime form P. Click any label round the matrix to give the selected voice that form: left edge P, top I, right R, bottom RI. Select a voice with 1 to 4 or by clicking its card. The circle at the right fills one pitch class at a time and flashes when all twelve have sounded: that is an aggregate. Press C to pair voice 2 with a form whose first six notes are exactly the six notes voice 1 leaves out, then listen to the aggregates close twice as fast. Click two notes in THE ROW to swap them and the whole matrix rebuilds.
try: Load a felt piano, a clarinet or flute, a pizzicato or plucked bass and a bell (single notes recorded at C) from your Splice folder into voices 1 to 4, choose the Berg row, set voice 1 to trichords and hear the major and minor triads hiding inside a twelve-tone row.

Choose the Webern Op. 21 row, switch on Klangfarben (K) and set every voice to single notes with a wide register spread: one line passed between instruments, note by note, as in Webern's orchestration.
Swap two notes of the row and watch the interval chart: try to build your own all-interval row (all eleven bars different heights), then press C and see whether it is combinatorial.

manifesto.name: Composition with twelve tones related only with one another
manifesto.author: Arnold Schoenberg (1874 to 1951)
